title: Protect me with your hand
hookLine: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe (Chaupai)

cards: In Punjabi, there's an old way of saying I'll stand by you: I've taken your arm. It's a promise, the kind you don't walk away from.
It's what a family does for a newcomer, an elder for a frightened child, a friend when your life falls apart. Not a handshake. A grip.
And it's the first picture in the Tenth Guru's prayer for protection, the very first thing it asks for.

teach.b: The line is hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Hamree: mine, our. Karo: make, do.
Haath dai: giving your hand. Rachhaa: protection, guarding. Protect me, giving me your hand.
Rachhaa is the poem's form of raksha, protection, the word also used for protective threads and amulets.

teach.h: NOT A CHARM, BUT A HAND.
teach.b: But the line asks for something else: a hand. Not an object to carry around, but the protector, reaching in. The Guru isn't asking for a charm; he's asking to be held.
Sikh teaching often points away from charms like these and toward the One, directly. Why a hand? Because a hand is personal.
An army can protect you. A wall can protect you.

But only someone right there, close enough to touch, can give you their hand. The line asks God to be that near. And it asks it of someone who sees everything, as later lines say, so it isn't a request to be noticed.
It's a request to be held, while noticed. Near its close, this same prayer returns to the picture from the hook: the one who has taken my arm. We'll get there on day three hundred seventy-eight.
For now, just the first line. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa.

how: Many Sikhs recite this opening line of Chaupai Sahib each morning and evening, and some say it on its own as a short prayer before a journey or a difficult moment.

a promise sealed with a handshake

games.q: the first line of Chaupai — tap the pairs.
p: a promise to stand by them

s: the first line asks for a protective charm or amulet
it asks for a hand, the protector reaching in, not an object to carry.
rachhaa is the poem's form of raksha, protection
the same word names threads and amulets tied for protection; the line asks for the One instead.
Chaupai only uses the hand picture once
it opens with a hand and, near its close, returns to the one who has taken my arm.

games.q: you're afraid and you want protection. you could ask for a wall, an army, or a charm. what does Chaupai's first line ask for?
o: a hand: protect me, giving me your hand.
games.why: hamree karo haath dai rachhaa: protect me, giving me your hand. not an object, but the protector near enough to touch.

practice: Place one hand flat on the center of your chest and feel its warmth and weight, and the heartbeat or the breath underneath. Let the hand do what a hand does: steady you.
If you pray, say the line, hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, or simply Waheguru; if not, let yourself be held for a minute, even by your own hand.

wordCard.voice: Rachhaa, protection. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa: the first line of Chaupai, asking not for a charm but for a hand, someone near enough to hold you.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: protect me, giving your hand. the opening line of Chaupai Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: keep me by the hand. Not a charm, a hand. That's one line; more tomorrow.
